name: Assadism
summary: Assadism is the governing doctrine of the Assad family's rule in Syria (1970-2024), a neo-Ba'athist system that kept the language of Arab nationalism and socialism while concentrating power in a dominant president, the Ba'ath Party and the security services. It pairs a secular state and a planned, nationalised economy with a leader cult, a strong military and intelligence apparatus, and hostility to Zionism, political Islam and independent opposition. Economic socialism gave way to selective liberalisation from the 1990s, while the authoritarian core stayed.
scope: The regime ideology of Hafez al-Assad (1970-2000) and Bashar al-Assad (2000-2024), as set out in the 1973 constitution and scholarly accounts; it answers as a loyalist of the ruling Ba'ath party-state would. It excludes the classical Ba'athism of Aflaq and al-Bitar, Salah Jadid's radical Marxist-Leninist phase, and the Iraqi Ba'ath branch, and treats later market-opening as a pragmatic adjustment rather than doctrine.

furtherReading.note: Accessible account of Hafez al-Assad's rule, party, religion and foreign policy up to the late 1980s.

furtherReading.title: Syria: Constitution of 1973 (Bern ICL)

keyFigures.name: Hafez al-Assad
keyFigures.role: Ruled Syria 1971-2000 and founded the regime's system and ideology.

keyFigures.name: Bashar al-Assad
keyFigures.role: Succeeded his father in 2000 and led the regime until its fall in 2024.

sources.title: Assadism
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Overview of the regime's nationalism, secularism, authoritarianism, economy, minorities policy, foreign policy and leader cult, drawn from cited scholarship.

sources.title: Syria: Constitution of 1973
sources.author: Syrian Arab Republic (text hosted by University of Bern, ICL)
sources.usedFor: Ba'ath leadership (Art. 8), planned socialist economy and property (Arts. 13-16), religion (Art. 3, 35), presidential and military powers, conscription, women, rights qualified by law.

sources.title: The Assad Era, in Syria: A Country Study
sources.author: Library of Congress Federal Research Division
sources.usedFor: Party control, security state, Islamist uprising and Hama, sectarian tension, Israel, Soviet alignment, civil liberties.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The Ba'athist state presented itself as socialist and provided public health services, though the constitution's explicit social guarantees are about work and education rather than healthcare.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Not discussed in the sources; inferred from the planned socialist economy and the state's role as main employer and wage-setter.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Art. 13 commits to a planned socialist economy and the state dominated industry, although the regime later opened to private investment and monopolised sectors through patronage.

public-ownership.rationale: Art. 14 names public ownership of natural resources and utilities as a form of property, and the regime nationalised banks, oil, power and about 90% of large industry.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Never a stated theme; inferred from socialist rhetoric, tempered by the regime's crony ties to a new business elite.

unions-good.rationale: Unions existed only as party-controlled popular organisations that mobilised and policed workers, so adherents back them as state organs but not as independent bodies.

property-fundamental.rationale: Art. 15 allows individual property to be expropriated for the public interest with compensation, and Art. 16 caps agricultural holdings, so property is protected but subordinate.

regulate-corporations.rationale: State planning controlled commerce and the regime kept policy control over private firms even after infitah, though regulation also served patronage.

cut-welfare.rationale: Inferred from the socialist state framework and subsidies; austerity came from fiscal strain, not doctrine.

worker-ownership.rationale: Art. 14 recognises collective ownership through cooperatives but the model is state ownership run by the party, not worker self-management.

surveillance-ok.rationale: The mukhabarat security services monitored political activity pervasively and the regime justified repression as defence against terrorists and Islamist insurgents.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Not discussed; a conservative-authoritarian security state would be expected to prohibit drugs.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Sectarian incitement was criminalised in the name of national unity, but this is inferred and was mostly used against opponents.

strong-leader.rationale: The regime centred on a dominant president with sweeping powers under Arts. 93-113 and a cult of the leader, and presented the leader as the guarantor of national unity.

state-harmful.rationale: Scholars describe a totalitarian system in which the Ba'ath Party controlled political, social, cultural and religious life, so a state-hostile view is the opposite of its doctrine.

limit-guns.rationale: Inferred: the regime monopolised arms and armed only loyal paramilitaries.

empower-police-military.rationale: Heavy military spending, a coup-proof security state and the armed forces' constitutional duty (Art. 11) to protect the revolution show strong commitment.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Not discussed; secular but socially conservative state with religious family law.

decide-locally.rationale: Power was centralised in the presidency and party, with security and appointments controlled from Damascus.

rehabilitation.rationale: Repression relied on harsh punishment, torture, disappearances and capital offences, as in making Brotherhood membership punishable by death.

traditional-family.rationale: The regime cultivated social conservatism and religious family courts while expanding women's public roles; support is moderate.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Sharia-based personal status law and a conservative social order leave no room for it, though the sources do not address it directly.

abortion-legal.rationale: Inferred from conservative family law and state pronatalism; not documented.

more-religion-public.rationale: Assad reversed Jadid's anti-religion drive but kept a secular state and refused tolerance of political Islam, while using quasi-religious rhetoric for the leader.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Not an issue for the ideology; its own treatment of Kurds involved Arabisation, so adherents reject remedial programmes.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Not addressed; the regime promoted women's participation but did not adopt constructivist theory.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Syrian Arab nationalism and Ba'athist indoctrination in schools and youth organisations stress national culture and Arab heritage.

gradual-change.rationale: The regime was revolutionary by origin yet institutionally conservative once in power; adherents are split.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Not a regime issue; inferred as indifferent.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The regime was anti-imperialist and defended sovereignty, and distrusted Western-led institutions.

free-trade.rationale: Planned economy, state control of commerce and protectionism marked the doctrine; liberalisation after 1991 was a pragmatic turn, not a principle.

nation-first.rationale: Sovereignty and regime survival came first in practice, even over pan-Arab goals, as shown by wars with Iraq and intervention in Lebanon.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: The regime rejected foreign intervention as imperialism, a stance central to its response to the uprising after 2011.

open-borders.rationale: Art. 1 insists territory cannot be ceded and the state is built on a national, security-minded sovereignty.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Not an issue in the sources; a statist developmentalist regime could favour state action, but oil revenue and industrial growth cut against it.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Inferred from the modernising, developmentalist self-image of the state; the sources do not discuss technology.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Not addressed; Syria's alleged nuclear programme was covert.

revolution-justified.rationale: The Ba'ath rose by coups and defines the state as protecting the revolution's goals (Art. 11), but denies the right of others to revolt against it.

experts-over-public.rationale: Technocratic and party vanguard rule is implied but public opinion is not formally ranked.

central-planning.rationale: Art. 13(1) defines the state economy as a planned socialist economy, which the regime practised, although it later liberalised.

socialized-markets.rationale: The regime accepted a private sector alongside public and cooperative ownership under party control; adherents split between statist and pragmatic views.

land-value-tax.rationale: Not discussed; inferred as foreign to the doctrine.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Inferred from the socialist aim of ending exploitation and land-ownership caps; inheritance tax is not documented.

basic-income.rationale: Not discussed; the regime used subsidies and patronage instead.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Import substitution and state control of commerce were standard policy through the 1980s.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The planned economy under Art. 13 and the public sector directed investment, and later investment rules kept policy in party hands.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Art. 14 gives public and collective ownership equal standing with individual property, and Art. 16 caps farm holdings, but the state, not small owners, anchors the economy.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: The planned socialist economy of Art. 13 kept money, wages and state salaries; no source shows any aim of abolishing them.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: State-run banks were nationalised and monetary policy was a state function.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Popular organisations for workers, peasants and professions were party-led bodies for mobilising and controlling society.

one-party-rule.rationale: Art. 8 names the Ba'ath Party the leading party in society and the state, and Art. 84 has it nominate the president.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: A republic, though hereditary succession from Hafez to Bashar shows adherents accept dynastic rule in practice, which is not a monarchy.

democracy-best.rationale: The constitution calls Syria 'democratic, popular, socialist' but elections were plebiscites; rhetoric favours 'popular democracy' over pluralist choice.

direct-votes.rationale: Referendums were used for approval of the president, but legislation was not decided by direct vote.

workers-councils.rationale: Political power rests in the party and presidency; popular organisations are subordinate.

right-to-secede.rationale: Art. 1 declares territory inalienable and the regime fought separatism and Kurdish autonomy.

natural-rulers.rationale: The doctrine does not claim natural rank, though the cult presented the leader as exceptional.

political-violence-never.rationale: The regime itself used massacres at Hama and Aleppo and justified force against opponents.

war-builds-character.rationale: Not stated as a principle, though military mobilisation is valorised.

separate-church-state.rationale: The state is secular and crushes political Islam, yet Art. 3 requires a Muslim president and Islamic jurisprudence as a main source of legislation.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Art. 3(2) makes Islamic jurisprudence only a main source of legislation; civil and criminal cases were handled by secular courts.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The regime kept courts, security services and arms entirely in the state (Art. 103 makes the president supreme commander), and extended party control over all institutions.

military-superiority.rationale: Syria sought strategic parity with Israel and armed heavily with Soviet help.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Official identity is Arab, not ethnic, and religious minorities were embraced rhetorically while Kurds were repressed.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Marxist-Leninist radicalism under Jadid was dropped by Assad, who kept socialist economic language but moved to a national unity framing.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Art. 13 aims to end exploitation but no stated equal-outcomes goal; privilege flowed to loyalists.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Not relevant; Kurdish land was seized in the Arab Belt.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Anti-imperialist rhetoric implies sympathy, not documented.

civilizational-union.rationale: Arab unity is a stated objective (Art. 1, preamble), though practised in a symbolic form.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The ideology is collectivist and appeals to national solidarity.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Constitutional rights are granted 'in accordance with the law' and subordinated to the revolution's goals and national unity, so duty to the state comes first.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: The sources never discuss environmental ethics; a developmentalist state is indifferent.

limit-population.rationale: Not addressed; a pro-military developmentalist state tends to favour population growth.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The regime pursued industrialisation and nationalised industry as progress.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Inferred: a regime focused on stability and control would not welcome disruption of institutions.

human-enhancement.rationale: Not addressed; conservative social order assumed.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Not addressed; rule is personal and party-based.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: The security state monitored communications and political activity.

restore-past-order.rationale: Presents itself as progressive and revolutionary rather than restorationist.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Assad's pragmatism, shifting from Leninism to infitah, suggests adherents judge by regime survival.

direct-action.rationale: The regime suppressed independent organising and treated street politics as sedition.

means-match-ends.rationale: The regime openly used coercion in service of national goals.

return-to-foraging.rationale: The doctrine pursued industrialisation, planning and nationalised industry; no source suggests any anti-civilisation strand.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: The planned industrial economy relied on specialised labour; no such utopian aim.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Socialist rhetoric but no stated distribution principle beyond ending exploitation.

production-for-use.rationale: Art. 13 describes a planned socialist economy aimed at ending exploitation, which implies production for social needs.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Art. 13 speaks of ending exploitation but the regime never adopted a labour theory of profit; its elite went into business.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Assad abandoned Jadid's Marxist-Leninist radicalism in favour of a nationalist party-state.

collective-farming.rationale: Land reform redistributed land to farmers; Art. 14-16 favour cooperatives and individual holdings, not full collectivisation.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Anti-imperialist rhetoric exists but the regime has no developed theory of this.

taxation-theft.rationale: A state-run planned economy with public ownership depends on state revenue, and no source shows any hostility to taxation.

harm-principle.rationale: Security services policed political and social activity and the regime justified restrictions by national unity and order, not only by harm to others.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The constitution protects personal freedom but ranks national unity and the revolution first, and recognises collective and religious communities.

conscription.rationale: Art. 40(2) makes military service compulsory; youth bodies gave military training.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Not addressed; the state restricted travel and treated emigres as suspect.

state-as-business.rationale: Not addressed; contrary to the statist ethos.

positive-liberty.rationale: The constitution links freedom to socialist goals, but not through explicit philosophy.

media-academia-power.rationale: The regime controlled media and universities itself.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Racial science is not part of Arab nationalist doctrine; inferred.

organic-representation.rationale: Popular organisations of peasants, workers and professionals were tied into the Progressive National Front led by the party.

total-state.rationale: The party's control reached into political, social, cultural and religious life, and scholars describe the system as totalitarian.

national-rebirth.rationale: Ba'athism carries the 'Arab renaissance' theme, though the Assad regime used it mostly as legitimacy rhetoric.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Foreign policy aimed at influence in Lebanon and regaining the Golan, not formal annexation, apart from the Greater Syria rhetoric.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Power rested on personal loyalty networks of Alawite and family clients installed in the army and security services.

bound-labor.rationale: Land reform redistributed about 85% of farmland and Art. 16 caps holdings, the opposite of binding farmers to a lord.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Not addressed; though schools were openly ideological.

universal-morality.rationale: Ba'athist doctrine is nationalist, with no stated universalist moral epistemology; adherents are indifferent.

single-common-good.rationale: Unity-oriented rhetoric of the nation and party as sole definer of the common good, inferred.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: The regime officially opposed Zionism and Israel, and the constitution's preamble condemns Zionism.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Not addressed except for Palestinian return.

revive-national-language.rationale: Not an issue; Arabic is the national language.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Workplaces were run through party-led popular organisations, not elected workers.

school-vouchers.rationale: Schools were government-run and promoted Ba'athist ideology, so private-choice funding conflicts with the system.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: The state ran deficits and heavy military spending; not an ideological stance.

economic-freedom.rationale: The regime held that political order and state control matter; economic liberalisation was selective.

rule-by-example.rationale: The cult stressed leader's virtue but the regime relied on laws and force.

national-self-determination.rationale: Anti-colonial and self-determination rhetoric for Arabs and Palestinians; denied to Kurds inside Syria.

force-without-un.rationale: Syria intervened in Lebanon and Jordan without UN sanction, but it condemned others doing so.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Secular state but promotes Islam and Christianity in schools.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Inferred from the nationalist framing; subsidies were mainly for citizens.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Constitutional language ties social rights to work, but state subsidies were broad; no stated conditionality.

class-collaboration.rationale: Under Assad class conflict gave way to national unity and a broad patriotic front under party leadership.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Ba'athist education promoted national and Arab heritage; sacrificing it is the opposite.

dominated-front.rationale: Syria led an anti-Western alignment with Iran and the Soviet bloc, later the Axis of Resistance.

workers-nation.rationale: Workers were organised through national party-led unions.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Art. 45 guarantees women equal opportunities in public life, and the regime conscripted women in the 1980s for a time.

ban-interest.rationale: A state-run banking system charged interest and the regime was secular.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Official identity is Arab and civic, and the constitution speaks of equal rights, though Kurds were discriminated against on ethnic and language grounds.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Doctrine is nationalist-socialist, not a Marxist state theory.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Oil was nationalised and a source of state revenue.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Arabisation of non-Arab minorities points to assimilationist attitudes.

elite-replacement.rationale: The regime's conspiracy narratives focused on Islamist and foreign plots, not on migration; inferred.

proportional-representation.rationale: Seat allocation inside a front dominated by the Ba'ath, not proportional.

national-mission.rationale: Ba'athist Arab mission is stated in preamble, but pushing the system abroad was not practised.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Official line is that women have equal opportunity (Art. 45).

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The regime denied its own elite's corruption and launched campaigns against selected cases.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Eugenics is not part of Arab nationalist doctrine; inferred rejection.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: The regime committed massacres at Hama and widespread disappearances and offered no accountability.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Art. 13(1) mandates a planned socialist economy and Art. 14 makes public ownership a basic form of property, so a minimal state is the opposite.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Not an element of Arab nationalism as practised.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Constitutional text states equal rights, though practice favoured loyal communities.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Assad dropped internationalist revolution for a national project.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: The regime and the preamble describe Israel and Zionism as imperialist.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Sharia courts handled personal status and non-Muslim communities had their own courts.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Religious conversion is not addressed in the sources, and sharia courts govern personal status.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Meat from cattle is part of ordinary Syrian life under a secular state and Muslim-majority society; inferred from absence of any such law.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: State schools provided mandatory religious instruction in Islam and Christianity, as the regime's secularism was not anti-religious.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: The regime justified a strong state by external threats.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Official rhetoric claimed popular legitimacy through plebiscites, but legitimacy was in practice party, army and security.

trade-surplus.rationale: Inferred from the protectionist, import-substituting economic management; not stated.

population-transfer.rationale: The Arab Belt deported tens of thousands of Kurds in 1973-76.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Doctrine and practice accepted force against internal opponents (Hama 1982) and external military intervention (Lebanon).

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Socialist and nationalist rhetoric prefers unity.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Political Islam was outlawed and Brotherhood membership was a capital offence.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Contradicted by arbitrary power of the security services.

separated-powers.rationale: Presidency controlled legislature, executive and judiciary (Arts. 93-113).

vanguard-party.rationale: The Ba'ath Party was the state's vanguard party and Art. 8 makes it the leading party.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Rhetoric of socialism and land reform favours peasants.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Art. 14-15 allow individual property, but public housing sales are not documented.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Unions were party-controlled organs for mobilising workers, leaving no room for independent strikes.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Regime blamed economic mismanagement and foreign pressure rather than numbers; inferred.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Rhetoric stressed unity of sects, while the regime manipulated sectarianism.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Government and military posts were reserved for party members and loyal elites rather than drawn by lot.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: A state of emergency from 1963 persisted for decades, and Art. 113 allows extraordinary presidential measures.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: State control of commerce included price setting and subsidies.

party-controls-media.rationale: The party and state controlled media and propagated the cult.

party-commands-army.rationale: Government and military posts went to party members, and Art. 11 charges the army with protecting the revolution's goals.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: The sources are silent; Syria was a country of emigration and refugees, and naturalisation was not an ideological matter.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: The ruling elite became wealthy through patronage.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Party membership gave control of state posts and the Ba'ath served as the vanguard; strict discipline is implied but not documented in detail.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Sovereignty prized, apart from the Arab unity aim.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Art. 103 makes the president supreme commander.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Churches had their own religious courts and hierarchies, but the doctrine takes no position on church government.

clerical-rule.rationale: The 1973 constitution is secular in orientation and political Islam was repressed and not tolerated.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Art. 11 charges the army with defending the revolution and the state, and loyalty to the state in war was a core demand of the regime's nationalism.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Censorship served regime control; moral wording inferred.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: The president's seven-year terms were renewable and Hafez al-Assad ruled until death in 2000.

recall-officials.rationale: Officials were accountable upward to the party.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Syria held a treaty with the USSR and an alliance with Iran.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Art. 15 protects individual property and nothing indicates a policy of banning renting.

people-in-arms.rationale: The regime relied on a standing army and loyal paramilitaries.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Peasants were favoured in land reform but no ideology of rural virtue.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Arab unity aim; Syria also claims Lebanon and the Golan.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: The party built its base on education and bureaucracy, so adherents resist this distrust.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Arab nationalism stresses the Arab nation's distinct heritage, yet the regime also proclaimed respect for all faiths; adherents are split.

death-penalty.rationale: Brotherhood membership was punishable by death and public hangings were used.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Art. 45 on women's participation, no stated curriculum position.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: State schools taught mandatory religion, though evolution policy is not documented; inferred.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Inferred from the socially conservative state and censorship apparatus.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Arab nationality tied to descent; stateless Kurds lacked citizenship after the 1962 census.

minority-language-support.rationale: Kurdish language was banned in schools and publications, Decree 768 banned Kurdish media.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Non-Muslim communities had separate religious courts, but no general exemption.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Conformity enforced by party and youth organs.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Nationalisation of banks, oil and industry presented as completing independence.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Constitutions were issued by the party-led leadership.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The regime justified restrictions as necessary for revolution and development.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Inferred from anti-imperialism and Syria's own dependence on foreign aid; not stated.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Strategic parity with Israel was a goal.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The president was chosen in a referendum after party nomination (Art. 84).

central-bank-independence.rationale: Banks were nationalised under state control.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Assad signed the 1974 disengagement and negotiated for land-for-peace, demanding return of the Golan.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Art. 15 permits expropriation in the public interest.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Syria was within the Soviet bloc and modelled the personality cult on Stalinist practice.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental regulation was not an ideological issue in the sources.

collective-defense.rationale: Syria sought alliances with the USSR and Iran, and the preamble says a threat to one Arab country threatens all.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Israel's 1981 annexation of the Golan was rejected; Syria demands its return.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The state kept religious institutions under control and refused independent Islamic political actors.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The president was nominated by the Ba'ath regional command (Art. 84) and led the party, so a non-partisan head is the opposite.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Art. 1 says territory may not be ceded, and the regime used force against internal rebellion.

region-keeps-system.rationale: A highly centralised unitary state; Syria's treatment of Kurdish and other regional demands shows no tolerance for regional special systems.

sacred-ruler.rationale: The cult cast the president in quasi-religious terms with sanctified titles, though not divine descent.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Inferred from the socialist state and its aim to end exploitation, which favours progressive taxation.

character-from-environment.rationale: Education and youth organisations were used to mould citizens.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Presidential powers were wide and the regime's leaders acted without legal restraint.

mixed-constitution.rationale: The constitution concentrates power in one president and one party rather than balancing few and many.

leader-cult.rationale: The regime built a cult with statues, portraits and mass praise of Hafez and Bashar al-Assad.

equal-parenting.rationale: Personal status was governed by sharia courts, which favoured traditional custody rules; inferred.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: The regime denied party leaders restored capitalism; it deprecated class struggle.

land-redistribution.rationale: About 85% of agricultural land was redistributed in land reform, and Art. 16 caps holdings.

refugee-return.rationale: Regime supports the Palestinian cause including return.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Greater Syria and Lebanon claims partly rest on national kinship.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: The state was secular in law and Art. 35 guarantees freedom of faith, although sharia courts governed family matters.

women-must-cover.rationale: The regime was secular and promoted women in public roles; compulsory covering was never policy in the sources.

common-currency.rationale: Arab unity was a stated goal but a shared currency was never documented in the sources.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Arab unity is declared even though practice was symbolic.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Not covered in the sources; the regime backed Palestinian return while minorities within Syria were told to integrate.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Marxist-Leninist under Jadid, dropped under Assad; no settled position.

ban-cartels.rationale: The state itself monopolised large parts of the economy via patronage.

no-bailouts.rationale: State-centred economy would support rescuing firms; inferred.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Courts were subordinate to the presidency and party; majoritarian legitimacy claimed.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Art. 45 promises women participation, but no quotas are documented in the sources.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Import substitution and Soviet-bloc trade, but also Arab economic integration rhetoric.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Trade standards were not an ideological issue; the regime opposed Western conditionality, but protected labour in rhetoric.

moral-incentives.rationale: Not addressed; the regime relied on patronage.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Ba'athists took power through coups, but adherents deny rebellion by others.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The regime itself passed office from father to son and held Alawite clan privilege.

history-own-civilization.rationale: School curricula promoted Ba'athist and Arab national history.

patriotic-education.rationale: School curricula and youth bodies promoted Ba'athist ideology and loyalty, with songs of praise in classrooms.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: No ideological stake in the debate; inferred as indifferent.

public-money-creation.rationale: State-owned banks and public control of finance.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Ba'ath doctrine does not predict capitalism's collapse, and the regime later liberalised toward capitalist practices.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Syria pursued influence in Lebanon and the Levant as a regional power.

delink-world-market.rationale: The regime integrated into the Soviet bloc, then opened to foreign investment.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: The doctrine contains no theory of labour aristocracy under Assad, who dropped Marxist-Leninist analysis.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: State law, not private choice, governed society.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The constitution guaranteed rights only 'in accordance with the law' (e.g. Art. 38, 39).

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Syria rejected borders drawn by France and Britain in Ba'athist doctrine.

elective-rulers.rationale: Elected in name via referendum, yet rule was hereditary in practice.

minority-veto.rationale: Decisions were taken by the president and party with no veto for dissenters.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The regime treated all opposition as treason or terrorism and killed tens of thousands to defend the ruler's position.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The People's Assembly was subordinate to the president (Arts. 98, 107, 111).

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: No documented position; neither promoted nor opposed.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Inferred: conventional use of animals is uncontroversial in the regime's social conservatism.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: The regime's rhetoric spoke of serving the masses, while elites took privilege; adherents are divided.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The party demanded mass mobilisation, though passivity was the real expectation.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: The regime itself used media for propaganda.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Not covered; though regime propaganda aimed at consent, it also relied on force.

party-own-road.rationale: Assad reoriented Syria away from Jadid's line to a national path.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: The economy depended on Soviet and Gulf aid.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Syria demanded return of the Golan and claims over Lebanon and Alexandretta.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: The doctrine's national identity is Arab and the regime rejected special political status for non-Arab peoples; inferred.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Not covered by the sources; Ba'athism has a nationalist rather than anti-fascist founding story.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Rejects a Western framing that condemns the Soviet bloc partner.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: The regime's cult statues and monuments were central; adherents defend honouring them.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: The regime rejected Western liberal democracy as unsuited to Syria, calling its own order popular democracy.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Art. 11 gives the armed forces responsibility for protecting the revolution's goals of unity, freedom and socialism, a political role beyond defence.

paid-care-work.rationale: Art. 45 promises women opportunity for public participation but not payment for domestic work.

filial-duty.rationale: Inferred from the conservative social order.

office-by-exam.rationale: Posts went to loyal party members and kin.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Nationalisation and state control of strategic industry.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Sharia courts handled family matters, which require grounds; inferred.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Officials were accountable upward to the party and president, not to voters.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Banks were nationalised and the state ran social provision.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Art. 14 recognises public, collective and individual ownership.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Art. 111 lets the president legislate when the Assembly is not sitting, so budget control is unclear in the sources.

single-official-language.rationale: Arabic was the sole language of public life and Kurdish was banned.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Inferred from the sovereignty emphasis and the limits on ownership, but not documented.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: No documented position; the state does not frame inequality in racial-disparity terms.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Socialist rhetoric suggests sympathy while the elite lived lavishly; adherents are split.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Syria backed Amal, Hamas and other armed groups and was accused of sponsoring terrorism.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Syria intervened militarily in Lebanon despite varied consent.

corporate-influence.rationale: Business influence was exercised through regime patronage rather than lobbying; the sources do not address it.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: The regime treated foreign-backed opposition as conspiracy.

job-guarantee.rationale: The public sector was a major employer under a planned socialist economy.

democratic-peace.rationale: Not addressed; contradicts anti-imperialist view of Western democracies.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: The regime demanded obedience through a coup-proof security system and the cult of the leader.

non-intervention.rationale: Non-interference and sovereignty were central to the regime's response to foreign involvement, even though it intervened itself.

industrial-unions.rationale: Unions were party-organised but the sources do not say how.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: The regime blamed Islamist and foreign plots; against minority specifics.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Personal status law was run by sharia and religious courts, so marriage was a legal institution.

public-access-to-information.rationale: The state controlled media and information and punished dissent; Art. 38 allows free expression only 'in accordance with the law'.

local-production.rationale: Import substitution favoured domestic production, but there is no local-economy doctrine.

informal-organisation.rationale: Independent organisations were suppressed and political life was channelled through party-led fronts.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Sovereignty is guarded in Art. 1 and the regime resisted outside intervention, though it also invoked international law over the Golan.

religious-nation.rationale: The nation is defined as Arab and secular though the president must be Muslim.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Syria deferred in practice to the USSR, but the doctrine rejects ritual tribute.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Centralised state, e.g. oil revenue held by Damascus.

defeat-communism.rationale: Syria was within the Soviet bloc and signed a 1980 friendship treaty with the USSR.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Public services were provided by the state sector within the planned economy.

religion-illusion.rationale: Assad reversed Jadid's anti-religious campaign and Art. 35 respects religion.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: The regime's rhetoric condemned capitalism while its later economic policy embraced investment.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Art. 45 speaks of guarantees but not economic transformation.

socialized-care.rationale: Art. 45 on women's participation hints at support, but the sources show no public care programme.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Arabic language was central, yet no purge campaign is documented.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Cooperatives exist but within a centralised plan.

majority-settlement.rationale: The Arab Belt policy settled Arabs in Kurdish Hasakah.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Ba'athism claimed a distinct Arab socialist road, not Marxism or capitalism.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Syrian claims to the Golan and Greater Syria.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Not a position of the regime in the sources; Syria's hostility is to Zionism, which it frames politically.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Inferred: Syrian law criminalised same-sex relations, but the sources do not state adherents' view.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Opposition was crushed, with mass killings and disappearances.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: The state was secular and ruled out blasphemy trials by religious authorities while keeping some religion-protecting laws.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The doctrine is anti-colonial and anti-imperialist.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: The regime used resistance rhetoric but not as religious obligation.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: This is the claim of the Islamist uprising that the regime crushed at Hama, and it held that its own rule was legitimate.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Participation was channelled through party fronts.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Not part of Ba'athist doctrine, which treats unity as primary; inferred.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Conservative social order; not addressed in sources.

assisted-dying.rationale: Inferred from the religious and conservative social order.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: The regime uses both socialist and nationalist language; no documented stance.

alienated-labor.rationale: Marxist analysis was dropped by Assad; no stated position.

islam-incompatible.rationale: The population is largely Muslim and the regime courted Islam.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The constitution derives authority from the people but the cult uses religious language.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Policy swung by period (restrictions on the veil in the 2010s, and none earlier); the doctrine takes no stable position.

social-market-economy.rationale: Post-1991 liberalisation partly fits; not doctrine.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Art. 11 defines the armed forces as protector of the revolution, Art. 40 makes service compulsory, and the army underpinned the regime.

rich-first.rationale: The infitah allowed a well-connected business class to enrich first, but doctrine still speaks of ending exploitation.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Syria aligned with the Soviet bloc, signing a 1980 friendship treaty, and later with Iran.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Bashar al-Assad succeeded his father Hafez al-Assad in 2000 after the minimum age was lowered, making dynastic succession a defining feature of the regime.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Never discussed; the planned economy had state-owned banks, but user-owned credit mutuals are not a regime theme.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Inferred from the regime's anti-Western, sovereignty-centred rhetoric and state-run economy, though the regime also opened its economy selectively.

property-franchise.rationale: The 1973 constitution provides universal suffrage in form, and the Ba'ath party presented itself as a mass party of workers and peasants.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Not part of the doctrine; the regime promoted women's formal equality but no such theory is attested.

reification.rationale: A Western Marxist concept the regime never used; its socialist rhetoric was official and simplified.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Inferred from the state's Ba'athist socialist rhetoric and from the state ownership of the press, though the regime's own control of media is the contrary practice.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Rule relied on emergency law in force from 1963, security courts and presidential decree, not on constraint by standing laws.

racial-franchise.rationale: The regime's official ideology was Arab nationalist and secular, and the constitution gives all citizens the vote and office in form.

online-participation.rationale: Inferred from the regime's control over public debate and its suspicion of independent politics; it did not support open citizen deliberation.

open-government-data.rationale: The security state kept decision-making secret and punished independent scrutiny.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: The state is officially secular, though personal-status law is by sect and Muslim women could not marry non-Muslims; the regime did not campaign on it.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: The regime posed as protector of minorities and officially opposed sectarianism.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Politics were managed by the president, the Ba'ath party and its front parties, leaving no room for independent citizen bodies with power.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Inferred from the secular modernising state and its control of the religious establishment, which favoured an official, state-friendly Islam.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The 1973 constitution and official Ba'athist socialism presented concentrated private wealth as hostile to the people, though in practice regime-linked fortunes grew.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Inferred: Syrian law criminalises homosexual acts and the regime never discussed military service, so an adherent opposes it.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The regime was secular but not atheist: it co-opted clergy and the constitution keeps Islam central, so state promotion of atheism was not its policy.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: The regime rested on an extensive police, intelligence and prison system that it saw as essential to protecting the state.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: The constitution makes the Ba'ath Party the leader of state and society and the regime officially denied sectarian shares, though it relied on loyal minority elites in practice.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: A state-led, planned economy and subsidies were the official model for helping the poor, with charity secondary.

term-limits.rationale: The president is elected for renewable seven-year terms with no limit, and Hafez al-Assad ruled for 30 years before his son succeeded him.

vote-delegation.rationale: Inferred from the one-party order, which kept decisions with the president and party and rejected independent political activity.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Anachronistic: the regime never addressed extinction risk, and its priorities were security and regime survival, so this is inferred.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Inferred: the regime appointed an all-male religious establishment and left religious offices to the confessions, without challenging male reservation.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: The constitution promises women equality, but personal status law keeps male household authority, and the regime kept both; adherents are not clearly one side.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Not addressed; the 1973 constitution speaks of citizens' rights and the regime's nationalism was Arab-centred, so non-citizen voting is inferred to be rejected.

rent-control.rationale: Not stated; inferred from the planned socialist economy and state control over housing and prices.

abolish-ip.rationale: Never addressed; inferred from a state-planned economy and tight control over information and culture.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Wikipedia's account of Assadism describes the Revolutionary Youth Union drilling students in ideology, a militarised society and military parades.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; the regime opposed Israel's arsenal but relied on Soviet and Russian protection.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Rhetorically anti-imperialist and sovereignty-minded, but it allied with the Soviet Union and later Russia; inferred and tempered by that alignment.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; adherents would have no settled doctrine on state recognition of genocide.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: The constitution's socialist economy and the regime's socialist rhetoric favour pay for work over property income, though the regime's crony elite earned rents.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: The regime was a heavily militarised security state that used force against opponents, as at Hama, and conscription is a constitutional duty.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Ba'athist doctrine holds a single Arab nation with an eternal mission, which the regime inherited.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Not addressed; the regime was secular but socially conservative, so inferred as rejecting the claim.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: Art. 45 guarantees women participation, and the regime ran state women's organisations under party control; inferred that adherents ground women's status in a shared category.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Inferred from the regime's military and leader-cult culture, which honoured fallen soldiers as martyrs; not stated in the sources opened.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: The regime was a secular Ba'athist state that justified rule by nationalism, socialism and security, not cosmic struggle.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Inferred from Ba'athist pan-Arab unity, which sought one Arab state rather than a homeland serving a diaspora.

culture-before-state.rationale: Inferred from the regime's state-first approach: party-state control of culture, education and religion.

god-not-male.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the regime's conventional, state-managed approach to religion.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Not addressed; the constitution makes Islamic jurisprudence a source of legislation and the regime policed religious reform.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Doctrine was state ownership and Arab unity, and the regime's patronage favoured loyalists across communities, not a stated majority-run economy.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: The regime suppressed Kurdish autonomy demands and pursued Arabisation; a merged ethnic region is inferred to be rejected.

independent-unions.rationale: Under Article 8 the Ba'ath Party leads state and society, and mass organisations such as unions operated under party control rather than independently.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Inferred: the regime called its state-run planned economy socialist while real power sat with the president and party, so a loyalist would reject the condition.

local-essentials-public.rationale: The constitution makes public ownership of basic resources and services the core of the planned economy, though it is national rather than local.

second-chamber.rationale: Inferred: the 1973 constitution vests legislation in a single People's Council under a dominant president; no second chamber is discussed in the sources.

municipal-property.rationale: Public property under the constitution is state property under central planning, and the doctrine is centralist.

confederal-coordination.rationale: The regime concentrated authority in the president, the party and the security services, leaving no room for local assemblies to decide.

family-wage.rationale: Inferred: the constitution's state protection of the family and its state-set wage economy point to support, but the sources do not discuss family wages.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Never discussed in the sources; no stance can be inferred.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Never discussed in the sources; no stance can be inferred.

anonymous-payments.rationale: A security state that watched and punished independent activity would not accept payments beyond state tracing.

online-anonymity.rationale: Inferred from the surveillance-oriented security state described in the sources; the internet is not discussed there.

person-over-state.rationale: The leader cult, the security services and rights qualified by law put the state and the leader above the individual.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The regime was secular but respected religion in the constitution; no clear stance on politics serving spiritual needs.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Inferred: Syria is a unitary, highly centralised state in which any regional power would be wholly at the centre's disposal.

gm-crops.rationale: Never discussed; no stance can be inferred.

dense-cities.rationale: Never discussed; no stance can be inferred.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Inferred: the regime's Arab nationalism and official non-sectarianism rejected organising by race or sect, though it favoured its own base in practice.

racial-pride.rationale: Inferred: Arab nationalism took pride in Arab identity and heritage, though the sources frame it as nation rather than race.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: The regime framed its wars as resistance to Israel, yet it also intervened in Lebanon, so a loyalist answer is not settled.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Ba'athist doctrine, which the regime kept, defines the Arab nation by shared language and history across state borders.

communal-electorates.rationale: The regime upheld a secular state and Arab-nationalist citizenship and opposed sectarian politics, so separate religious electorates contradict it.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Regime rhetoric routinely blamed Western, Israeli and Gulf plots for threatening Syria, as scholarly accounts of its conspiracy framing describe.

free-public-college.rationale: The socialist state provided free public education including universities, in line with its constitutional commitment to education.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Inferred from a planned, state-owned economy that used direct control rather than market pricing and gave little weight to environmental policy.

future-generations.rationale: Not discussed; inferred from the regime's state-development and nationalist rhetoric, which accepts duties to future national generations.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Inferred from the regime's secular-socialist stress on equal citizenship; it did not claim a distinct women's outlook should be weighted in politics.

arms-reduction.rationale: The regime built a very large military and pursued strategic parity with Israel, so cutting forces to a minimum ran against its policy.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Inferred from a security state that conducted foreign policy through the presidency and intelligence services, usually in confidence.

capital-controls.rationale: A planned, nationalised economy kept state control over foreign exchange and capital movement, which persisted despite later selective liberalisation.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Armed forces and security services are the core of the regime, and the party-state allowed no independent armed opposition, so a state monopoly on arms fits.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: The 1973 constitution makes military service a sacred duty and the regime relied on conscription, so refusing orders is against it.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Unions were brought under Ba'ath party control as popular organizations, so independent bargaining with employers did not fit the system.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: The socialist state set wages and subsidies by planning; tax credits are inferred as outside its model.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Inferred from a state-planned economy and a dominant president with wide control over the budget; the sources record no view on borrowing limits.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: The regime used Arab nationalist and anti-imperialist rhetoric that favored a fairer world order, but the sources do not state this as a policy.

smash-state-machine.rationale: The regime's aim was to hold and expand state power through the party and security services, not to break up the state apparatus.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: The 1973 constitution sets out a planned socialist economy with state direction, leaving no room for free experiment with other systems.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Ecological accounting is anachronistic and was not part of Ba'athist doctrine; inferred from its state-planned development focus.

sacred-nation.rationale: The regime kept Arab nationalism and treated the Arab nation as a unity with a historic mission, though its actual rule was centred on the Assad family and party.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Education was state-provided and fees were low, so relief is inferred as consistent; student loans are not documented.

internal-colonialism.rationale: The regime held that the party-state served all regions equally, so a charge of internal colonialism would be rejected; inferred.

shared-human-nature.rationale: The regime was secular and socialist but the sources record no stance on a fixed human nature.

public-service-media.rationale: Media were owned and directed by the party-state and civil liberties were limited by law, so media free of government control are against the system.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Inferred as indifferent: the regime was secular and courted minorities, but the 1973 constitution made Islamic jurisprudence a source of law and took no stand on religions' unity.

farm-price-support.rationale: Inferred from the planned socialist economy and agrarian reform in the 1973 constitution; the state set crop prices and ran farm credit and cooperatives.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Inferred from the regime's emphasis on strategic deterrence against Israel and a strong military; Syria had no such weapons, so this is anachronistic.

workers-own-party.rationale: The Ba'ath party held the leading role under Article 8 and independent political parties were suppressed, so a loyalist rejects a separate working-class party.

ban-fgm.rationale: Inferred from the regime's secular modernising self-image and stated equality for women; FGM was not a regime issue.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Inferred from personal status law drawn from Islamic jurisprudence, which gave women smaller inheritance shares, even though the constitution states equal rights.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Not a regime issue; Arab nationalism stressed Arabic as the national language but the statement is about how a language is named.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Inferred from a state-run economy where agencies and the party, not private courts, handled harm.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Inferred from the centralised party-state, which co-opted tribal sheikhs informally but gave no chiefs an official law-making role.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Inferred as indifferent: the regime restricted liberty for security and party reasons, not for the environment.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Not discussed in the sources; courts were subordinate to the presidency and security services, so fixed sentences were not a stated position.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Inferred from Arab nationalism's stress on Arabic as the national language, giving a loyalist reason to expect newcomers to learn it.

missingStatements.text: A state may be led by one family, with the presidency passing from parent to child.
missingStatements.rationale: Bashar al-Assad succeeded Hafez al-Assad in 2000 after the constitution's minimum age was lowered, making dynastic succession a defining feature of the regime.

missingStatements.text: Ethnic and religious minorities should be favoured in the armed forces and security services so they can protect the state from the majority.
missingStatements.rationale: The regime installed loyal Alawite elites in the army and security services as a coup-proofing system, though it officially denied sectarianism.
missingStatements.declined: Specific to the Assad regime's coup-proofing; not a question other ideologies would meaningfully answer, and the bank is kept lean.

missingStatements.text: The state should arrange to keep the country's non-state armed allies abroad as a deterrent against stronger rivals.
missingStatements.rationale: Syria cultivated allies such as Hezbollah, Hamas and Iran as the 'Axis of Resistance' to offset Israel's superior power.

notes: Assadism is mostly a regime-practice doctrine, so many answers rest on documented practice and constitutional text rather than manifestos. Hafez's phase (Leninist-socialist, then infitah) and Bashar's more liberalising phase differ on markets; the profile reflects the stable core. Jadid-era Marxism and original Aflaq Ba'athism would answer differently on religion, class struggle and pan-Arab unity.
